name: SQL and AI Training Data Pipelines
title: SQL and AI Training Data Pipelines
answer: Training and fine tuning data inside an organisation is usually assembled by pipelines that extract rows from operational databases, clean and join them with SQL, and load them where training jobs can read them. Mistakes in those queries become mistakes in the model. This page covers the SQL layer of that work, from source tables to the feature and label tables that training jobs consume. It sits in the AI and SQL field, alongside data engineering and model evaluation.

sections.body: Training and fine tuning data inside an organisation is usually assembled by pipelines that extract rows from operational databases, clean and join them with SQL, and load them where training jobs can read them. Mistakes in those queries become mistakes in the model. This page covers the SQL layer of that work, from source tables to the feature and label tables that training jobs consume. It sits in the AI and SQL field, alongside data engineering and model evaluation.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Pipelines run on the database engines that hold the source data, commonly PostgreSQL, MySQL, or a warehouse such as Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift. Orchestration is handled by schedulers like Airflow or dbt, and increasingly by Model Context Protocol servers that let AI agents query SQL systems directly; this site tracks 263 such servers for SQL databases and warehouses. Storage for intermediate tables may sit in the warehouse, in object storage, or in a feature store. The choice of engine shapes what SQL the pipeline can use and how expensive each run is.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is mostly SQL: SELECT statements that join operational tables, filter bad rows, deduplicate records, and compute labels or features. Engineers write these queries as versioned files, often with dbt or a similar tool, and run tests for nulls, duplicates, and unexpected row counts before the data is promoted. Time based splits and point in time joins are used to keep the training set from leaking information that would not be available at prediction time. The output is a table or set of files that a training job reads, and the query that produced it is part of the model's provenance.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Because training data often contains personal or licensed information, pipelines need access controls, column level masking, and a record of which rows were used for which model. Provenance is kept by versioning both the SQL and the resulting dataset, so a model can be traced back to the queries and source tables that produced it. Teams commonly review data rights before extraction, check for consent or contractual limits, and document any filtering of sensitive fields. Poorly governed pipelines can leak personal data into a model or train on data the organisation has no right to use, and the query log is often the first place an audit looks.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more automated pipeline construction, with language models drafting SQL and agents using MCP servers to inspect schemas and propose joins. Data contracts and declarative transformations are gaining ground, so that the same query logic can run across engines without rewriting. Provenance and data quality checks are moving earlier in the pipeline, before training starts, rather than being patched after a model fails. The site's library of 288 research papers and 732 AI tools reflects how quickly this area is changing, though the core work remains SQL that has to be correct.
